issue.description:
src/service/leases.rs:248-303 (validate_lease_for_mutation): when no ACTIVE lease matches (issue, current assignee), the mere existence of ANY historical lease row (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM leases WHERE issue_id = ?) raises Error::LeaseExpired. Lease rows are never deleted: release_issue_impl/close_issue_impl (src/service/lifecycle.rs:344-436) do not purge them and cleanup_expired_leases (leases.rs:342) is #[allow(dead_code)], never called. All four lifecycle ops call validate_lease_for_mutation whenever the issue has an assignee (lifecycle.rs:47,102,142,176).

Net effect: once an issue has EVER been claimed with --lease-ttl, any later NON-leased claimant is permanently locked out of close/release/update — the issue is stuck in_progress+assigned forever (the classic fleet-starvation shape) with no CLI recovery path (update --clear-assignee hits the same validation).

Reproduced live at HEAD (dac3910): 'bead claim --assignee w1 --lease-ttl 30' -> 'bead release <id>' -> 'bead claim --assignee w2' (plain) -> 'bead close <id> --reason done' fails exit 4 'Lease for issue ... has expired or is invalid for assignee w2'; release and update fail identically.

Fix options (pick one, document in the close reason): purge the issue's lease rows on release/close; or scope the 'lease existed' check to the current assignment epoch (e.g. leases created at/after the current claim event); or treat expired/foreign lease rows as absent when the current claim was non-leased.

Acceptance (run in repo):
1. Script the repro above in a temp workspace; w2's close now succeeds exit 0.
2. Active-holder fencing is unchanged: existing tests/r002_leased_claims.rs pass.
3. Regression test added to tests/r002_leased_claims.rs covering leased-claim -> release -> plain-claim -> close; cargo test passes.

issue.description:
check_dependency_graph() in src/service/doctor.rs queries:

  SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT blocked_id) FROM dependencies

The dependencies table has no blocked_id column -- it is blocked_issue_id
(blocked_issue_id, blocker_issue_id, kind, condition). The query therefore
fails to prepare on every invocation, and the surrounding .unwrap_or(0)
swallows the error, so the diagnostic line reports '0 blocked issues'
unconditionally, in every workspace, regardless of the real value.

REPRODUCTION (tradegraph workspace, 454 dependency rows):
  $ bead doctor
    OK dependency_graph: Dependency graph OK: 454 dependencies, 0 blocked issues, no cycles
  $ sqlite3 .beads/beads.db 'SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT blocked_id) FROM dependencies'
    Error: no such column: blocked_id
  $ sqlite3 .beads/beads.db 'SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT blocked_issue_id) FROM dependencies'
    176

'454 dependencies, 0 blocked issues' is internally impossible -- nonzero
dependency rows cannot yield zero distinct blocked ids -- which is what makes
this visible at all.

IMPACT
A health-check line that is silently and permanently zero. An operator reading
'0 blocked issues' next to a nonzero dependency count may conclude nothing is
blocked, which is the opposite of what the store says.

SCOPE
- Correct the column to blocked_issue_id.
- Restrict to kind = 'blocks': the line is labelled 'blocked issues', and
  relates_to edges are informational and do not block.
- Do not swallow the error. This query failing should be loud; .unwrap_or(0)
  on a diagnostic turns a broken check into a passing one.

NOTE
An audit of all 24 SQL literals in doctor.rs against a real store found this
is the only one that fails to prepare. The other .unwrap_or(0) sites are
latent risk of the same class, not currently wrong -- consider them
separately rather than in this fix.

issue.description:
## Summary

`bead update <id> --notes "..."` reports success and bumps the issue revision,
but the note text is not persisted anywhere. It is not in the SQLite store, not
in the checkpoint, and not in `bead show --json` — there is no `notes` field at
all, and `comments` stays empty.

This is silent data loss on a **documented** flag. `bead update --help` lists it
under both EXAMPLES and OPTIONS:

    bead update ID --notes "Investigated root cause"   # Add investigation notes
    --notes <NOTES>    New notes

Version: bead 0.1.3.

## Reproduction (isolated, empty workspace)

    mkdir /tmp/repro && cd /tmp/repro && git init -q .
    bead init --prefix repro
    ID=$(bead create --title repro --priority 3)
    bead update "$ID" --notes "SENTINEL_NOTE_VALUE_12345"; echo "rc=$?"
    bead show "$ID" --json
    grep -r SENTINEL_NOTE_VALUE_12345 .

Observed:

- `rc=0`
- `bead show --json` returns keys: assignee, comments, created_at,
  dependencies, description, id, labels, priority, revision, status, title,
  updated_at. No `notes`. `comments` is `[]`.
- `revision` goes 1 -> 2 and `updated_at` advances, so a mutation WAS committed.
- The sentinel string appears in **no file in the workspace** — not
  `.beads/beads.db`, not `.beads/checkpoint/`.

## Why this is worse than a missing feature

The revision bump is the dangerous part. A caller that writes a note and then
checks 'did my update apply?' sees a changed revision and concludes yes. Any
optimistic-concurrency caller using `--if-revision` also burns a revision for
a write that stored nothing.

This bit in practice while filing declarat-751aca4f in declarative-config: a
correction was attached with `--notes`, appeared to succeed, and was gone.
Because `bead update` also cannot change a description, the only recovery was
to close that bead and recreate it — so the failure mode costs a bead ID and
leaves a spurious closed issue behind.

## Expected

One of, in order of preference:

1. Persist the note — expose it as a `notes` field on the issue and in
   `show --json`, and include it in the checkpoint so it survives a rebuild.
2. Append it as a comment, since `comments` already exists in the schema and is
   the natural home for investigation notes.
3. If `--notes` is genuinely not implemented, make it a hard usage error and
   remove it from `--help`. A flag that exits 0 and does nothing is the worst
   of the three.

## Acceptance criteria

- The reproduction above finds the sentinel after the update, via
  `bead show --json` and in the checkpoint.
- A regression test asserts a note round-trips through
  create -> update --notes -> show, and through a checkpoint flush + rebuild.
- No revision is consumed by an update that stores nothing.

issue.description:
cmd_init returns early on WorkspaceState::Ready, before reaching apply_migrations. Nothing else in the CLI applies a pending migration to an existing store: doctor --repair does not create tables, and no migrate subcommand exists.

CONSEQUENCE
Installing a newer binary over an older store leaves every workspace short of
the tables the new code queries. The failure is deferred to whichever command
touches one first and surfaces as a bare SQLite error that names neither the
schema version nor a remedy:

  $ bead list --ready
  bead: SQLite error: no such table: issue_resource_keys

OBSERVED ON EX44
A binary built 2026-08-17 sat at schema v9 while the current binary expects
v13 (issue_resource_keys arrives in the 10..13 range). Upgrading broke 'bead
list --ready' and 'bead claim' -- the core of the NEEDLE fleet loop -- across
62 of 63 workspaces simultaneously. 'bead doctor' still passed, because it
touches none of the new tables, so the store looked healthy while the frontier
was unreadable.

'bead init' printing 'Workspace already exists' and exiting 0 is what makes
this hard to diagnose: the documented recovery path reports success without
doing anything.

FIX
init applies pending migrations when the workspace is Ready, reporting
'Applied pending migrations: schema N -> M' or 'Schema up to date (version N)'.
Migrations are versioned and idempotent, so this is safe to run unconditionally
and is what the init help text already promises ('Repeated initialization with
the same prefix is safe and deterministic').

Deliberately NOT auto-migrating on every store open: a partial upgrade racing
several live workers is a worse failure than an explicit repair step, and
CLAUDE.md already documents 'bead init' as the schema-rebuild path.

FOLLOW-UP WORTH CONSIDERING SEPARATELY
Commands that fail on a missing table could compare the store's
schema_migrations version against CURRENT_VERSION and say 'workspace is at
schema 9, this binary expects 13 -- run bead init' instead of surfacing raw
SQLite text.

issue.description:
## Problem

bead claim has no check for whether the requesting assignee already holds an in_progress issue elsewhere in the same workspace. This lets one assignee accumulate unbounded simultaneous in_progress claims with no upper limit.

Real incident (2026-08-17, commitgraph workspace, a NEEDLE-fleet consumer of bead-rs): one assignee (claude-code-glm-5-commitgraph-2) held 9 simultaneous in_progress beads, another (claude-code-glm-5-adr018) held 8. All 25 in_progress beads in that workspace were confirmed stale (no live process working the repo; last real file touch predated even the freshest claim's updated_at) and released by hand. Ready frontier went 0 -> 22 after release.

## Proposed behavior

Add an opt-in claim-time guard, following the same per-call opt-in pattern leasing already uses (src/service/leases.rs: DEFAULT_LEASE_TTL/MIN_LEASE_TTL/MAX_LEASE_TTL are caller-supplied via the existing --lease-ttl flag on bead claim, not stored workspace config -- this should work the same way, not as a .beads/config.json default).

Proposed flag: bead claim --assignee X --single-claim (name TBD). When set, claim_issue (src/service/claim.rs:130) checks -- within the same transaction, same workspace database, before find_eligible_issue (claim.rs:638) / find_eligible_frontier (claim.rs:829) run -- whether X already has any issue with base status in_progress in this workspace. If so, refuse with a new ReasonCode (e.g. AssigneeHasActiveClaim) naming the blocking issue ID, rather than proceeding to select and assign a new one.

Scoped to this workspace's own database only. bead-rs stores are already one-per-workspace (one beads.db per repo), so this is a same-transaction query against the local issues table -- no cross-workspace lookup is needed or possible, and none is wanted: the point is per-workspace containment, not a global assignee registry.

## What this does and doesn't fix

Bounds impact, does not eliminate staleness. An assignee can still abandon their one claim and let it go stale -- this guard doesn't detect or reap that, it only prevents accumulation. With it, the ceiling is 1 stale claim per assignee per workspace, not unbounded.

Complementary to, not a replacement for:
- needle-d9a36be9 (NEEDLE): mend's own-newer-claim detection heuristic -- backstop for whatever still goes stale within the ceiling of 1
- Adopting the existing --lease-ttl mechanism in NEEDLE's claim path -- bounds how long that 1 stale claim can persist before another worker can reclaim it

## Scope: only the claim action itself

Applies only to the path where claim_issue / claim_issue_with_lease / claim_issue_with_policy newly assigns a previously-unassigned ready issue to an assignee -- i.e. where the assignee relationship is first established by a claim. Does NOT apply to other paths that set an assignee on an issue, e.g. bead update --assignee on an already-open issue. That is a distinct, already-tracked bug shape (NEEDLE bead needle-44e7e5cd: open+assignee issues invisible to the ready frontier, not a real active claim) with different consequences and should not be entangled with this guard.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] New opt-in flag on bead claim (e.g. --single-claim); default behavior unchanged when the flag is omitted
- [ ] With the flag set, claim fails with a distinct, machine-readable reason (new ReasonCode) when the assignee already holds an in_progress issue in this workspace, naming the blocking issue ID
- [ ] The check runs inside the same atomic transaction as selection/assignment -- no race between check and assign
- [ ] Does not alter bead update --assignee behavior on open issues
- [ ] Fixture: assignee holds one in_progress issue; bead claim --single-claim for the same assignee returns AssigneeHasActiveClaim and assigns nothing; after releasing or closing that issue, the same assignee can claim normally again

issue.description:
Discovered while fixing beadrs-98f229c0 (pragma-configured connections, shipped in 4d08718): SQLite does not invoke the busy handler when a connection holding a read snapshot -- a DEFERRED transaction that has already executed a read -- attempts to upgrade to a write transaction. That upgrade returns immediate SQLITE_BUSY regardless of busy_timeout. Reproduced empirically: with one connection holding BEGIN IMMEDIATE, a second connection in a deferred BEGIN that has run a SELECT fails its next INSERT instantly (0.000s) despite busy_timeout=5000, while a fresh autocommit write on the same connection waits out the lock and succeeds.

Every mutating command path uses rusqlite unchecked_transaction() (deferred): lifecycle.rs (4x), recurrence.rs (3x), external_refs.rs (2x), data.rs (2x), dependencies.rs (5x), checkpoint.rs (several), main.rs cmd_create/cmd_claim. So even with the shared pragma opener in place, two fleet workers running bead claim/update concurrently against one workspace can still hit immediate 'database is locked' -> exit 1 on the read-to-write upgrade, undermining the README 'Coordinating a fleet' concurrency contract that beadrs-98f229c0 was meant to restore.

The one existing counterexample is checkpoint.rs execute_restore_into_empty, which already uses TransactionBehavior::Immediate and documents why: holding the write transaction before inspecting the target prevents races.

Fix: convert the mutating handlers' unchecked_transaction() calls to immediate transactions (Transaction::new_unchecked(conn, TransactionBehavior::Immediate) or unchecked_transaction_with_behavior), starting each write transaction before its first read so lock acquisition happens up front and busy_timeout actually governs contention.

Acceptance:
- a test where two connections (or two CLI invocations) contend on a mutating command demonstrates the loser waits via busy_timeout rather than failing immediately (contrast with the documented pre-fix behavior in tests/connection_pragmas.rs)
- no deferred read-then-write upgrade remains on any mutating command path
- cargo test passes

ADR-009 (2026-08-16) records that making bead-rs Git-aware — detecting unpulled
upstream changes to .beads/ before a flush — was considered and REJECTED, and
routes the underlying hazard here.

Rationale: R027 already states "bead-rs still never runs Git". Detecting the
store STATE (a verified checkpoint ahead of live) is strictly better than
detecting one transport: it is accurate regardless of how the checkpoint
arrived, and avoids importing Git's failure modes (detached heads, absent or
multiple remotes, shallow clones, worktrees, auth failures on a network probe)
into the flush path, where a false verdict from a safety check is worst.

rule remains unenforced operator discipline in Git-transported deployments, and
downstream documentation carries it as a standing rule. ADR-009 also asks that
R027's specification describe the Git-transported workflow it reconciles, so the
hazard is documented in-project rather than only downstream.

Authorized by: docs/adr/003-automatic-checkpoint-flush-gated-on-incremental-publication.md

## Overview
Make a successful semantic mutation publish a checkpoint generation covering its own committed sequence, replacing explicit sync flush-only as the default, so the durable checkpoint is never silently behind the database.

Gated. Per-mutation publication against the current path would write bytes quadratic in mutation count into a Git-tracked directory: flush is linear in workspace size, each generation leaks a full-workspace-sized object that is never collected, and most mutation kinds never advance the sequence that signals a flush is needed. The prerequisites are the implementation converging on plan sections 6.1.1 and 6.2 as already written; each is worth fixing whether or not the default ever changes.

bead-rs still never invokes Git. Automatic Git publication remains rejected.
